column2: In 1896 the archaeologist de Baye went down the Volga and up the Kama, crossed the Urals by rail to Tyumen, travelled by river to Tobolsk, Samarovo and the mouth of the Irtysh among the Ostyaks, then by tug to Tomsk and along the Trans-Siberian, then under construction, to Krasnoyarsk; he returned via Omsk, Kurgan and Orenburg.

In the winter of 1910 Asselin travelled on the Trans-Siberian from Moscow via Irkutsk, Baikal and Manchuria (Harbin) to Vladivostok, then by sea via Nagasaki to Shanghai and up the Yangtze to Chengdu, where he was going to take up a consular post.

In the winter of 1877 Ujfalvy travelled from Orenburg via Orsk, the Aral Sea, Kazalinsk and Turkestan to Tashkent, visited Khujand, Samarkand and Panjakent, and in the autumn returned via Verny, Kulja and Kopal, Sergiopol, Semipalatinsk, Omsk, Petropavlovsk and Troitsk to Orenburg. The book is mainly scientific (ethnography, archaeology) and travel details are scattered; the Fergana part is described in vol. I.
Kubalski's compilation: a retelling of Gmelin's journey through Siberia and of the memoirs of a Polish exile sent to Kamchatka; the author made no journey of his own.

Vol. 2 of Kittlitz's memoirs of the voyage of the sloop “Senyavin”: in the summer of 1828 the naturalist travelled from Petropavlovsk on horseback and by bat (dugout boat) via Nachiki, Malka, Ganaly and Pushchino down the Kamchatka River to Klyuchi and back, and in the autumn went via Apacha to Bolsheretsk and the west coast (Yavino, Golygino). The rest of the volume covers the Pacific islands and the return to Europe. OCR is damaged in places.

In 1911 the hunter E. von Kapherr travelled via St Petersburg, Vologda, Perm and Yekaterinburg, by steamer from Tyumen via Tobolsk to Repolovo and by boat up the Konda to the Shemini hunting grounds; in 1912 he hunted roe deer with his wife near Yekaterinburg (Istok, Kashino), and in 1913 he came to Kashino again. Most of the book consists of sketches of game, hunting and peoples.

In the summer of 1900 the Belgian journalist Tytgat travelled via Berlin, St Petersburg and Moscow on the Trans-Siberian to Irkutsk, across Baikal to Sretensk, by steamer down the Shilka and Amur past the banks devastated after the Blagoveshchensk massacre, then by train to Vladivostok and by sea via Nagasaki to Tianjin and Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion.

In the spring and summer of 1893 the medical missionary Wenyon travelled from Vladivostok by tarantass to Lake Khanka, by steamers along the Sungacha, Ussuri, Amur and Shilka to Sretensk, along the post road via Chita, Baikal, Irkutsk and Krasnoyarsk to Tomsk, by steamer to Tyumen and by train and along the Kama and Volga to Moscow and St Petersburg; at the border at Verzhbolovo he was briefly detained.

Bergman's Swedish expedition was shipwrecked off the south coast of Kamchatka in 1920 and reached Petropavlovsk; in the autumn Bergman and his wife sailed to Ust-Kamchatsk, wintered there and in January–April 1921 travelled on skis and by dog sledge along the Kamchatka valley back to Petropavlovsk. In the winter of 1921–1922 he went via Nachiki, Tolbachik and Kozyrevsk to the Lamuts, then via Klyuchi and the Yelovka pass to the west coast (Sedanka, Tigil) and along it south to Petropavlovsk.

In the winter of 1826 the botanist Ledebour, with Meyer and Bunge, travelled from Dorpat via St Petersburg, Moscow, Kazan, Perm, Yekaterinburg, Irbit, Tobolsk and Omsk to Barnaul, and from there to Zmeinogorsk, Kolyvan and Riddersk; in summer he made trips to Ust-Kamenogorsk, the sources of the Charysh and Uymon, along the Irtysh to Zyryanovsk and the Chinese picket on the Bukhtarma, and in autumn returned via Loktevsk to Barnaul and by the winter road to Dorpat. The Fraktur OCR is badly garbled.

In the summer of 1914 Lethbridge and his wife went from Vologda to Arkhangelsk, the Solovetsky Islands and the White Sea, then along the Sukhona to Veliky Ustyug, via Kotlas and Vyatka to Perm, along the Kama to Cherdyn, by the mining-works railway across the Urals to Verkhoturye and Yekaterinburg, via Tyumen to Omsk and by steamer along the Irtysh to Semipalatinsk; the outbreak of war caught them there, and they returned via Omsk to Petrograd.

In 1903 Lord Ronaldshay travelled by caravan from Cilicia via Aleppo, Mosul and Baghdad to Persia (Kermanshah, Tehran, Enzeli), via Baku and the Transcaspian railway to Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent, along the post road via Semirechye and Kulja to Semipalatinsk, hunted argali in the Altai near Kosh-Agach, went from Biysk by steamer along the Ob to Novo-Nikolayevsk and on the Trans-Siberian and the Chinese Eastern Railway — via Irkutsk, Baikal, Chita and Harbin — to Port Arthur and Beijing.

In the autumn of 1901 the journalist Fraser travelled by mail train from Moscow via Samara, Ufa and Chelyabinsk to Omsk, Tomsk and Irkutsk, crossed Baikal, went via Chita and Nerchinsk down the Amur to Blagoveshchensk and Khabarovsk, visited Vladivostok, then along the Chinese Eastern Railway under construction via Grodekovo, Harbin and Hailar returned to Transbaikalia and Irkutsk (visiting the Aleksandrovsky Central Prison) and left for Europe by train.

The merchant Dobell arrived in Petropavlovsk in the autumn of 1812 and went up the Kamchatka River to Nizhnekamchatsk; in the winter of 1813 he travelled by dog sledge through Klyuchi and the Koryak settlements to Kamenskoye and Gizhiga, then by reindeer and raft through the taiga to Okhotsk, in summer on horseback along the Yakutsk road to Yakutsk, up the Lena to Kachug and Irkutsk and on along the highway through Krasnoyarsk, Tomsk, Tobolsk, Tyumen and Yekaterinburg to Russia.

In the spring of 1910 Carruthers's expedition travelled by cart from the railway at Achinsk to Minusinsk, crossed the Sayans into the Uriankhai country (the basins of the Biy-Khem and Ulug-Khem), crossed the Tannu-Ola to the Mongolian plateau (Achit-Nur), went to Sharasume and Chuguchak, through the Dzungarian Gate to Kulja for the winter, and in 1911 travelled along the Imperial road to Urumqi and Guchen.

In 1879 the clergyman Lansdell, distributing the Scriptures in prisons, travelled from St Petersburg and Moscow along the Volga and Kama to Perm, via Nizhny Tagil and Yekaterinburg to Tyumen and Tobolsk, by steamer to Tomsk, made a trip to Barnaul, along the highway via Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk, across Baikal to Kyakhta and Maimachen, via Chita and Nerchinsk to the Kara goldfields, along the Shilka and Amur to Nikolayevsk, back to Khabarovsk, along the Ussuri, Sungacha and Khanka to Vladivostok and by sea to Japan.

In the autumn of 1898 Colquhoun travelled on the Siberian railway to its end near Irkutsk, along the “commercial road” to Kyakhta, via Maimachen, Urga and the Gobi to Kalgan and Beijing, then by sea to the Yangtze, up to Chongqing and via Guizhou and Yunnan down the Red River to Tonkin (1899).

In 1828 the astronomer Hansteen, with Erman and Due, travelled from St Petersburg via Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Perm and the Urals (Tagil, Verkhoturye) to Tobolsk, and in winter via Kolyvan, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk and Troitskosavsk near Kyakhta; in the spring of 1829 he went down the Angara and Yenisei to Turukhansk and back to Yeniseysk, then via Zmeinogorsk, Semipalatinsk, Zlatoust and Ufa to Orenburg, and in the winter of 1830 through the Kirghiz Steppe (the khan's residence), Astrakhan, Saratov and Penza back to St Petersburg.

In the summer of 1847 Hill travelled from Moscow via Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Perm, Yekaterinburg and Tyumen along the Ishim road to Tomsk, where he lived until winter; then via Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk, in the winter of 1848 across Baikal to Selenginsk, Kyakhta and Maimachen and to the Gusinoozersk datsan; in spring he went down the Lena to Yakutsk, rode the Yakutsk–Okhotsk road to Okhotsk and sailed on a government vessel to Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky.

In 1902 Gerrare travelled on the Trans-Siberian to Irkutsk, crossed Baikal, reached Sretensk, went down the Shilka and Amur on a private steamer to Blagoveshchensk and by mail steamer to Khabarovsk, then by train to Vladivostok; from there, using someone else's papers, he got into closed Manchuria via Nikolsk-Ussuriysky and Grodekovo and travelled on construction trains via Harbin and the Khingan to Hailar.

Radloff, who lived in Barnaul, made ten expeditions in 1860–1870: through the Altai mountains to the Chuya steppe and Kobdo, to Salair and Lake Teletskoye, to the Kulunda and Baraba steppes, through Semirechye to Verny, Kulja and Issyk-Kul, via Minusinsk and Krasnoyarsk through Yeniseysk province, along the Irtysh and Tobol to Tobolsk and Tyumen, and in 1868 to Tashkent and Samarkand. The routes are reconstructed from the author's list of journeys in the introduction (paragraphs 00054–00072).

The Polish exile Felińska was sent in March 1839 from Kyiv via Tula, Nizhny Novgorod and along the ice of the Volga to Kazan, via Perm and Yekaterinburg to Tyumen and Tobolsk, and in spring by barge along the Irtysh and Ob past Demyanskoye, Samarovo and Kondinsk to Beryozov, where she lived until 1841.

A book by two officers: in 1911 one of them travelled from Beijing via Kalgan and the Gobi along the telegraph line to Urga, then along the Mongolor stations to Kyakhta and via Selenginsk to Verkhneudinsk; in 1913 the other went from Shanghai via Beijing, Mukden and Harbin along the Chinese Eastern Railway and the Trans-Siberian to Verkhneudinsk, reached Urga via Kyakhta, travelled with the consul to Uliastai and Kobdo, and from there via Kosh-Agach and Onguday along the Chuya road to Biysk and by steamer to Barnaul and Novo-Nikolayevsk.

In 1917–1918 the war correspondent Grondijs was in Petrograd, on the South-Western Front and with Kornilov's forces on the Don, and returned via Petrograd to Paris; at the end of 1918 he came via Washington and Tokyo to Harbin, and after stops in Chita, Irkutsk and Omsk went to the Western Front of Kolchak's army (Chelyabinsk, Ufa, Sterlitamak, Krasnoufimsk); with the retreat he moved to Yekaterinburg and Omsk, in the summer of 1919 observed the fighting against partisans near Barnaul and Biysk, and in the autumn punitive operations on the Shilka near Zilovo and in Chita.

In September 1909 the author travelled from Korea via Andong, Mukden, Changchun and Harbin to Chita, by train to Sretensk, then by steamers along the Shilka and Amur to Blagoveshchensk and Khabarovsk and along the Ussuri Railway to Vladivostok. A two-day visit to Port Arthur is described separately.

In the summer of 1842 Simpson sailed from Sitka to Okhotsk, rode to Yakutsk, went up the Lena by boat to Kachug and via Irkutsk (with a trip to Baikal) travelled by post-horses along the Siberian highway via Krasnoyarsk, Tomsk, Omsk, Tobolsk, Yekaterinburg and Kazan to Moscow and St Petersburg.

In May–August 1881 Cotteau travelled by rail and along the Volga to Perm and Yekaterinburg, by tarantass to Tyumen, by steamer along the Tobol, Irtysh, Ob and Tom to Tomsk, along the highway to Irkutsk and Sretensk, then down the Amur to Khabarovka and along the Ussuri and Khanka to Vladivostok, from where he sailed to Nagasaki.

In the autumn of 1898 Reid travelled by caravan from Beijing via Kalgan, the Gobi and Urga to Kyakhta, on horseback to Baikal, crossed to Irkutsk and in 12 days travelled on the newly opened Siberian railway via Krasnoyarsk and Omsk to Chelyabinsk and Moscow.

The Bremen expedition of 1876 travelled by sledge via Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Perm and Yekaterinburg to Omsk, then via Semipalatinsk to Semirechye (Lepsinsk, Alakol), to Zaisan and the Altai, via Barnaul to Tomsk, by steamer down the Ob to Obdorsk, made a trip into the Yamal tundra and in the autumn returned via Tobolsk, Tyumen and Kazan to Moscow.

In 1902 a mining engineer travelled on the Trans-Siberian with detours to the goldfields of the Achinsk and Minusinsk districts, via Baikal and Transbaikalia to Sretensk, along the Amur to Nikolayevsk and the Amgun, by sea to Vladivostok and along the Chinese Eastern Railway back west; in 1903 he went again via Harbin and Vladivostok by sea to Olga and Tetyukhe. The text has noticeable OCR errors.

In the winter and spring of 1903 Turner travelled by train via Samara, Kurgan and Omsk to Novo-Nikolayevsk (with a detour to Tomsk), by sledge via Barnaul and Biysk into the Altai mountains as far as Katanda and the Belukha glacier, and after returning to Biysk left by train for Europe the same way.

After a short stay in Vladivostok in the autumn of 1880 and 8 months in Japan, in June 1881 Joest returned from Nagasaki to Vladivostok, went via Nikolskoye and Khanka down the Ussuri to Khabarovka, up the Amur to Sretensk and by tarantass via Chita, Verkhneudinsk (with an excursion to Kyakhta and Maimachen), Irkutsk, Tomsk and Shadrinsk to Yekaterinburg, Kazan and Moscow.

Atkinson travelled from Moscow via Kazan and Perm to Yekaterinburg, toured the Ural works, then through the Ishim steppe to Barnaul, the Altai and the Upper Irtysh; in later years he went to Lake Teletskoye, Mongolia, the Kirghiz Steppe and Semirechye, and then via Achinsk, the Sayans and Khövsgöl reached Baikal and Irkutsk. The chronology of the book is non-linear; the division into journeys is approximate.

In 1849–1850 Atkinson travelled from Ust-Kamenogorsk and Semipalatinsk via Ayaguz to Kopal and the Dzungarian Alatau, roaming among Kirghiz auls, and in October 1850 returned to Semipalatinsk; later, from Irkutsk, he explored Baikal and set off via Posolsk, the Selenga valley, Selenginsk and Petrovsky Zavod towards Nerchinsk. The description of the Amur in the second half of the book is a compilation, not a personal route.

In the spring of 1900 Meakin and her mother travelled along the Siberian railway via Omsk, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk (with a trip to Minusinsk) to Irkutsk, crossed Baikal, went by train to Sretensk, by steamers along the Amur to Blagoveshchensk and Khabarovsk, then to Vladivostok, from where they sailed to Japan and returned home via America.

In 1898 Stadling (searching for the Andrée expedition) travelled on the Trans-Siberian to Tulun, on horseback to Irkutsk and Zhigalovo, by steamer down the Lena to Yakutsk, Bulun and the delta, then by reindeer via the Olenyok, Anabar and Khatanga to the Yenisei at Dudinka, and via Turukhansk and Yeniseysk returned to Krasnoyarsk and Europe.

In the summer of 1882 the yacht “Marchesa” came from Hakodate to Petropavlovsk; Guillemard and his companions crossed Kamchatka overland via Nachiki, Ganaly and Milkovo and went down the Kamchatka River to Ust-Kamchatsk, then visited Bering Island on the yacht and returned via Petropavlovsk to Japan. The rest of the book describes a voyage around East Asia and the Malay Archipelago.

In the summer of 1929 Heller sailed on the icebreaker “Krasin” from Leningrad round Norway into the Kara Sea (anchoring off Vaygach), changed to a steamer and went up into the mouth of the Yenisei, visited Igarka and Dudinka, then on river steamers via Turukhansk and Yeniseysk reached Krasnoyarsk. A pilot's account of a flight from Dikson is someone else's route.

In the winter of 1869 Whyte crossed Mongolia from Tianjin and Beijing via Kalgan by camel with lamas to Maimachen and Kyakhta, then by sledge along the Siberian highway via Irkutsk, Krasnoyarsk, Tomsk, the Baraba steppe, Tyumen and Yekaterinburg to Perm, Kazan and Nizhny Novgorod.

In 1906 the hunter Niedieck came from Japan on the steamer “Stepney” to Petropavlovsk, hunted bears in Bechevinskaya and Morzhovaya bays, then went along the coast via the Karaginsky and Anadyr gulfs to the Gulf of the Cross in Chukotka and left for Nome; the rest of the book is about hunting in Alaska.

In the summer of 1908 the crew of the Italian car “Züst” in the New York–Paris race crossed from Japan to Vladivostok, drove through Manchuria to Nerchinsk and Chita, via Baikal (by ferry) and Irkutsk along the Siberian highway to Omsk, Tyumen, Yekaterinburg and Perm, then via Kazan, Nizhny Novgorod, Moscow, St Petersburg and Berlin finished in Paris.

In the winter of 1897 Jefferson and his companions travelled by train via Chelyabinsk, Kurgan and Omsk to the Ob, Taiga and Tomsk, then to the terminus at Krasnoyarsk, by sledge along the Yenisei to Minusinsk and Karatuz and to the goldfields in the Sayans (with a foray beyond the range); at the end of March they returned via Minusinsk and Achinsk and left by train for the west.

A whaler's ship's doctor spent five months whaling in the Tatar Strait and the Sea of Okhotsk, buried a sailor on the shore near Tauysk and then called at Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky before sailing to California. Most of the book consists of sketches of Kamchatka, its history and the defence of 1854, not a route.

In 1920 Ossendowski fled from Krasnoyarsk into the Yenisei taiga, went through the Minusinsk steppes and the Sayans into Uriankhai and Mongolia, visited Khövsgöl (Khatgal), by his own account the edge of Gansu, then Uliastai and Narabanchi, and in 1921 reached Urga via Zain-Shabi, from where he left for Beijing. The order of the middle part of the route (Khatgal–Uliastai) is confused in the book; the reliability of several episodes is disputed.

Lasies, a deputy and an officer of the French mission, arrived in Vladivostok at the end of 1918 and was in Yekaterinburg in December; in April–June 1919 he travelled by rail with General Janin from Vladivostok to Omsk, Yekaterinburg, Perm and the front at Vereshchagino and returned to Vladivostok, from where he left via Japan and America. The book is mainly political; travel details are scant.

In the summer of 1903 Swayne travelled by train from St Petersburg and Moscow via Chelyabinsk to Novo-Nikolayevsk, by steamer along the Ob to Barnaul and Biysk, along the Chuya road via Onguday to Kosh-Agach and hunted argali in the Mongolian Altai; in August he returned the same way to Biysk, Novo-Nikolayevsk and Moscow.

The book consists of sketches by a mining engineer who lived at copper mines in the Kirghiz Steppe; there is no continuous route, but individual trips are described: in 1904 via Chelyabinsk to Yekaterinburg, from Petropavlovsk by troika to the mines, in winter by sledge from Omsk to Pavlodar, and trips among the auls.

The prisoner of war Fuchs was sent in a troop train from Kyiv via Moscow, Perm, Omsk, Tomsk, Krasnoyarsk and Irkutsk to a camp near Vladivostok; in September 1916 he escaped, hid in Irkutsk and, posing as a Russian soldier, travelled via Tomsk, Chelyabinsk and Samara to Moscow and St Petersburg, and in 1917 escaped via the Caucasus, Persia and Kurdistan to Turkey and in June 1918 returned to Germany.

From Shanghai via Nagasaki and Korean ports (Seoul) by sea to Vladivostok, then in winter by sledge along the Ussuri and Amur, through Transbaikalia, Irkutsk and Tomsk to Tyumen; then by train and sledge across the Urals, via Kazan and Nizhny Novgorod to Moscow.

On foot and by any available transport from London via St Petersburg and Moscow to Siberia, with a detour to the Irtysh and the Altai, then along the Lena to Yakutsk, the Kolyma and via Oymyakon to Okhotsk and Kamchatka; back with his wife via Yakutsk, Irkutsk, Transbaikalia and Kyakhta to St Petersburg.

In the summer of 1896 along the Trans-Siberian, then under construction, to Krasnoyarsk, then along the highway via Irkutsk and Baikal to Transbaikalia to inspect the prisons of the Nerchinsk penal servitude; back to Tomsk and by river via Tobolsk to Tyumen and Perm.
A compilation on Siberia and the Northern Sea Route: long quotations from Wiggins, Sibiryakov, Nordenskiöld, Hill and others; the author made no journey of his own.

The first volume of the report on Humboldt's expedition of 1829: from Berlin via St Petersburg, Moscow and Kazan to the Urals (the works as far as Bogoslovsk), then via Tyumen and Tobolsk to the Altai and the Chinese post of Baty; the volume breaks off at Bukhtarminsk.

A biography of Captain J. Wiggins compiled by H. Johnson from his diaries and letters: voyages to the Kara Sea and the Yenisei (1874–1894) and Wiggins's sledge journey across Siberia; the author himself did not travel. Wiggins's route could be mapped separately if desired.

In the summer of 1890, to inspect prisons: from Paris via St Petersburg and Moscow, along the Volga and Kama to Perm, by train to Tyumen, then by steamer with a convict barge along the Tobol, Irtysh, Ob and Tom to Tomsk; back by steamer and post-horses to Tyumen.

In 1902 a Hungarian prelate travelled on the Trans-Siberian from St Petersburg to Irkutsk, across Baikal by ferry and along the Chinese Eastern Railway to Harbin, Mukden and Port Arthur, then via Tianjin to Beijing; later he visited Seoul and Japan.

In the summer and autumn of 1913 Nansen sailed on the steamer “Correct” through the Kara Sea to the mouth of the Yenisei, went up the Yenisei by launch to Yeniseysk, by tarantass to Krasnoyarsk, then along the Trans-Siberian and the Chinese Eastern Railway to Vladivostok and Khabarovsk, inspected the Amur Railway under construction and returned by train to European Russia.

In 1902 the Austrian Pistor travelled on the Trans-Siberian to Irkutsk, across Baikal to Kyakhta and Maimachin, on to Sretensk and by steamer along the Amur to Blagoveshchensk and Vladivostok; he then continued his round-the-world journey via Japan, China, Australia and Oceania (not mapped).

In 1887 the engineer Boulangier travelled on the Ural railway to Tyumen, by steamer along the Tobol, Irtysh, Ob and Tom to Tomsk, by tarantass along the highway to Irkutsk; from there he made trips along the Angara to Bratsk and Padun, to the Oka, to Zima, Usolye and the Aleksandrovsky Central Prison.

In 1897 Legras travelled by rail to Omsk and the Ob, lived in Tomsk, in spring went by steamer through the Ob–Yenisei Canal to Yeniseysk, then via Krasnoyarsk and Kansk to Irkutsk, Kyakhta and Transbaikalia; floating down the Ingoda and Amur he reached Khabarovsk, went along the Ussuri Railway to Vladivostok and sailed to Japan. The second half of the text is poor OCR.

A collection of essays on Siberia: the author describes a trip to the Barguzin peninsula via Tataurovo along the eastern shore of Baikal and a trip “peasant-fashion” from Irkutsk through Buryat villages of Transbaikalia to Selenginsk and Kyakhta; the other chapters deal with history and natural history.

In 1800 Kotzebue was arrested at the Russian border at Polangen and sent under escort via Mitau, Riga, Polotsk, Moscow, Kazan and Perm to Tobolsk, then into exile in Kurgan; after his pardon he returned via Tobolsk, Perm and Moscow to St Petersburg, from where he left for Livonia in the spring of 1801.

L. Atkinson's letters: with her husband from Moscow via Kazan and Yekaterinburg to Tomsk and Barnaul, to the Altai (Lake Teletskoye), via Ayaguz to Kopal in Semirechye and to the Lepsa; then via Barnaul, Tomsk, Krasnoyarsk and Minusinsk to Irkutsk, with trips from there to Kultuk and Kyakhta; in 1853 via Barnaul and Yekaterinburg to St Petersburg.

In the summer of 1890 Rabot travelled along the Volga and Kama to Perm and Cherdyn, crossed by portage to the Pechora, went up the Shchugor and crossed the Northern Urals to Lyapin, then down the Sosva and Ob via Beryozov to Samarovo and Tobolsk and returned via Tyumen and Yekaterinburg.

The ship's surgeon of HMS “Barracouta” describes the squadron's cruises during the Crimean War: Nagasaki and Hong Kong (1854), the occupation of Petropavlovsk, Ayan and the Amur estuary (1855), then the survey of the coast of the Tatar Strait and Primorye with calls at Hakodate, Korea and Nagasaki (1856).

In the winter of 1891 Kate Marsden travelled by sledge from Zlatoust via Tyumen, Tobolsk, Omsk and Tomsk to Irkutsk, sailed down the Lena to Yakutsk and in summer visited the leper colonies of the Vilyuy district on horseback; in autumn she returned the same way to Moscow and St Petersburg.

In the spring of 1877 the ornithologist H. Seebohm travelled by sledge across the Urals via Tyumen, Omsk and Tomsk to Krasnoyarsk and Yeniseysk, went down the Yenisei to where Wiggins's ship was wintering on the Kureika and in summer reached Golchikha; back by barge to Yeniseysk, then via Tomsk by steamer to Tyumen and along the Kama and Volga to Moscow.

Piotrowski, who had secretly returned to Poland, was arrested in Kamianets, and after the Kyiv fortress was sent under escort to Omsk and to the Yekaterininsky works near Tara; in 1846 he escaped via Irbit, the Urals, Solikamsk, Veliky Ustyug, Arkhangelsk and St Petersburg to Riga and via Germany to Paris.

In the summer of 1893 Helen Peel, on the yacht “Blencathra” as part of Wiggins's Kara expedition, sailed via Norway, Vardø and Yugorsky Shar through the Kara Sea to the mouth of the Yenisei and Golchikha; back via Arkhangelsk and the Norwegian fjords to Dundee. The chapters on Wiggins's journey across Siberia are not included.

In 1909 the officer P. Etherton travelled from Kashmir via Gilgit, Hunza and the Pamirs to Yarkand and Kashgar, then through Eastern Turkestan to Kucha and via Dzungaria to Chuguchak and Sharasume; in the winter of 1910 he went via Zaisan, Ust-Kamenogorsk and Barnaul to the Trans-Siberian at Novo-Nikolayevsk.

The Austrian officer and prisoner of war F. Wlad was sent along the Trans-Siberian to the Peschanka camp near Chita; after a failed escape attempt through Mongolia he fled to Manchuria (Harbin), reached the USA via China, Shanghai and Japan, but was detained by the British on his way to Europe.

Lieutenant W. Hooper of HMS “Plover” (the Franklin search) wintered in 1848–49 in Emma Harbour (Providence Bay) in Chukotka, making sledge trips to Chukchi settlements; in the summer of 1849 he passed through the Bering Strait to Point Barrow, by boat to the mouth of the Mackenzie, wintered at Fort Franklin and returned to England via Canada.

In the spring of 1910 the author took the Trans-Siberian from Moscow to Krasnoyarsk, then from Achinsk by tarantass across the Chulym and the Abakan steppe to Minusinsk. In summer he crossed the Sayans and spent time on the Kemchik and the upper Yenisei with Russian traders.

In the autumn of 1840 the author set out from Moscow via Orenburg and the line of fortresses to Petropavlovsk, Omsk, Semipalatinsk and the Altai works (Zmeinogorsk, Barnaul, Kuznetsk), wintered in Tomsk and reached Irkutsk. On the way back he travelled in the suite of Governor-General Rupert via Omsk, Yekaterinburg, Perm and Kazan to Moscow.

An analytical work with occasional travel notes: in the summer of 1897 the author travelled on the Trans-Siberian to Krasnoyarsk, then by tarantass via Irkutsk, the Khamar-Daban and Kyakhta to Chita, then along the Amur to Khabarovsk and on to Vladivostok. The route is reconstructed from scattered mentions; the order is partly conjectural.

In the autumn of 1901 the author took the Siberian Express from Moscow via the Urals, Chelyabinsk and Omsk to Irkutsk, saw the city and the prison, then went by special train to Baikal (Baranchiki, Listvenichnoye). The Siberian chapter is part of a larger book on Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

In the summer of 1901 the author arrived in Vladivostok, travelled along the Ussuri Railway to Khabarovsk and by steamer down the Amur to Nikolayevsk, from where he went to Sakhalin and spent 50 days studying the penal colony and the Gilyaks (floating down the Tym). In the autumn he returned to Vladivostok and along the unfinished Chinese Eastern Railway and the Trans-Siberian via Harbin, Chita, Baikal and Irkutsk reached Moscow.

The magnetic expedition of 1828–1829: from Berlin via St Petersburg, Moscow, Kazan and the Urals to Tobolsk, a winter journey along the Ob to Beryozov and Obdorsk, then along the highway via Tara, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk and Kyakhta. In the spring of 1829, along the ice of the Lena to Yakutsk and on horseback via the Aldan to Okhotsk.

Letters and reports of the linguistic expedition of 1845–1849: from Kazan via Perm and Tyumen to Tobolsk, along the Irtysh and Ob to Surgut and Narym, then Tomsk, Yeniseysk, Turukhansk and Dudinka. In 1847–1848, the Minusinsk basin and the Sayans, the Kansk district, Nizhneudinsk, Irkutsk, Kyakhta, the Nerchinsk works and Chita; back via Krasnoyarsk, Omsk and Ufa to St Petersburg.

In August 1913 Nansen sailed on the steamer “Correct” through the Kara Sea to the mouth of the Yenisei, then went up the Yenisei on the motor boat “Omul” to Yeniseysk and by horse to Krasnoyarsk. From there along the Trans-Siberian and the Chinese Eastern Railway via Irkutsk, Chita and Harbin to Vladivostok and Khabarovsk, along the Amur Railway under construction, and back via Chita, Irkutsk and the Urals to St Petersburg.

In 1823 the blind traveller Holman went from St Petersburg via Moscow, Kazan, Perm and Yekaterinburg to Tobolsk, then along the highway via Tara, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk. Suspected by the authorities, he was sent back with a state courier via Tomsk, Omsk, Perm, Kazan and Moscow to the Polish border.

In the summer of 1880 the author travelled along the Volga and Kama to Perm, along the Ural railway to Tagil and via Tyumen by steamer to Tobolsk, then by boat down the Irtysh and Ob via Samarovo and Beryozov to Obdorsk and the Gulf of Ob (Nipte, Yar-Sale). He went back up to Tobolsk and by tarantass via Kurgan, the Kirghiz steppe and Verkhneuralsk to Orenburg.

The Czekanowski and Müller expedition: in December 1873 from Irkutsk along the Lena to Kirensk, then to the Lower Tunguska (Yerbogachen) and by reindeer to the Olenyok, floating down the Olenyok to Ust-Olenskoye. In the autumn of 1874 across the tundra to the Lena (Siktyakh, Bulun), then via Verkhoyansk to Yakutsk and along the Lena back to Irkutsk (January 1875).

In 1902 a Danish journalist spent two months in Tyumen and Tobolsk, sailed to the Ostyaks as far as Samarovo, then via Tara to Omsk, along the Ob to Barnaul and Biysk, to the Altai (Chuya), to Tomsk and by rail to Irkutsk. After three weeks on Baikal: Kyakhta, Sretensk, the Amur to Khabarovsk, Vladivostok, by sea to Port Arthur, Manchuria and Beijing, and back along the Chinese Eastern Railway via Harbin and Irkutsk.

In 1890 the Faroese Patursson came across the Urals to Tyumen, went down the Irtysh and Ob by sloop to the Taz and lived for a year among the Samoyeds and Yuraks (trips to the Yenisei and Taimyr), then in winter returned with a caravan via Surgut to Tobolsk and Tyumen. After living in Tomsk and travelling to the Altai, in 1895 he took the highway to Irkutsk, floated down the Angara and Yenisei to Golchikha and returned to Europe by sea.

In the summer of 1914 the ornithologist Haviland, with Czaplicka's expedition, travelled by train to Krasnoyarsk and by steamer down the Yenisei via Yeniseysk, Turukhansk and Dudinka to Golchikha, where she spent two months. In September she returned by sea via Dikson and the Kara Sea to Norway and England.

In 1894 de Windt came to Sakhalin on a convict steamer and inspected the prisons of the Korsakovsky and Aleksandrovsky posts, Rykovskoye and Derbinskoye, then via Vladivostok along the Ussuri road reached Khabarovsk and along the Amur Sretensk. He visited Gorny Zerentui and Akatui, went back down the Amur to Nikolayevsk and left by sea.

In the summer of 1923 (according to the text, not 1918 as in the catalogue) the journalist travelled from Riga to Moscow and in the train of the Soviet ambassador Karakhan along the Trans-Siberian via Vyatka, Perm, Yekaterinburg, Omsk, Novonikolayevsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk and Verkhneudinsk to Chita. Then via Manchuria station, Harbin, Changchun and Mukden he reached Beijing.

A collection of Siberian sketches and other people's stories; the author's own path is hardly described, apart from his life as an exile in the village of Balakhta and a trip in July 186– from Minusinsk through Tatar uluses and the Sayans to the Chinese border.

A book about the round-the-world voyage of a Russian squadron; the Siberian episode is a call in the autumn of 1859 at De-Kastri Bay and the passage through the Amur estuary to Nikolayevsk and back, after which the ship left for Japan and then San Francisco.

In the spring and summer of 1896 Jefferson cycled from London via Hamburg, Riga, St Petersburg and Moscow, then along the Siberian highway via Kazan, Perm, Yekaterinburg, Ishim, Omsk, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk to Irkutsk (6,574 miles). From Irkutsk he made a steamer trip to Baikal (Listvenichnoye).

Notes by a member of the Anglo-French squadron of 1855: from Hakodate to De-Kastri Bay (the blockade of the Russian squadron), then Aniva Bay, the northern entrance to the Amur (Deception Bay) and the port of Ayan, where the author went ashore; back along Sakhalin to Japan and via Suez to England.

An Englishman serving in the German army was taken prisoner by the Russians in 1915 and sent in a troop train via Moscow to a camp in Sretensk. After the revolution he worked as a tutor in Irkutsk, then left by rail for Vladivostok; the train's route through Siberia is not given in detail.

The convoy route of the exile Giller in 1854: from the Warsaw citadel via Brest, Smolensk, Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, Perm and Yekaterinburg to the border of Tobolsk province (20 November). The Siberian part of the journey to the Nerchinsk region is not described in the book; the Lithuanian section (part II) is lost.

In the autumn of 1867 (according to the text; the catalogue gives 1856–1857) Bishop Sheepshanks travelled from Kalgan through Mongolia to Urga and Kyakhta, along the Selenga to the Posolsky Monastery on Baikal, crossed to Irkutsk and by tarantass via Tomsk and Omsk reached Perm, then along the Kama and Volga to Nizhny Novgorod, Moscow and St Petersburg.

Taken prisoner wounded in Courland in 1915, the author was sent via Mitau and Moscow to Nizhny Novgorod and the Totskoye camp near Orenburg, in the spring of 1916 by troop train along the Trans-Siberian to a camp near Irkutsk, then round Baikal via Verkhneudinsk to a Transbaikal camp. The names of the later camps and the escape route are not specified in the text.

In the summer of 1897 Baron de Baye, having studied the Mordvins near Penza, travelled via Yekaterinburg and along the Trans-Siberian via Chelyabinsk, Kurgan, Omsk and Novonikolayevsk to Taiga station with a detour to Tomsk, then to Krasnoyarsk. In August he went up the Yenisei by steamer to Minusinsk and returned via Krasnoyarsk to Moscow.
